tasks.title: Write a function that prints a message, then call it three times.
Rewrite a repeated block from an old script as a function.
Write a script with three functions that print your IP, your gateway and your DNS server.
Pass arguments into a function and use them inside it.
Make a function return success or failure, then act on the result with an if.
Write a function that checks whether a string looks like a valid IPv4 address.
Create an array of five hostnames and print each one with a loop.
Print how many items the array holds and access one item by index.
Store a list of subnets in an array and loop over them printing each one.
Do multiplication, division and modulo inside a script and print the results.
Write a function that returns how many hosts a given prefix length allows.
Write a script that prints a CIDR table from slash 24 to slash 30 with host counts.
Extract part of a string using bash parameter expansion.
Replace text inside a variable without calling any external command.
Write a function that splits an IP address into its four octets.
Capture the output of ip route into a variable and print it.
Extract only the default gateway address from that output.
Write a script that prints the gateway and warns if there is no default route.
Use awk inside a script to print a chosen column from a command's output.
Use awk to print only the lines where a column matches a condition.
Write a script that lists listening ports and the process for each, formatted neatly.
Use sed to replace text in a file and write the result to a new file.
Use sed to edit a file in place while keeping a backup copy.
Write a script that safely adds an entry to the hosts file if it is not already there.
Write a script that takes a domain and prints only its A record.
Extend it so a second argument chooses the record type, defaulting to A.
Add a usage message that prints when the script is run with no arguments.
Write a function that reports whether a given host and port are reachable.
Add a timeout so the check fails fast instead of hanging.
Make the script exit non zero when the port is closed so automation can use it.
Loop over a list of common ports and report which are open on one host.
Loop over a list of hosts and check one port on each.
Print a clean summary at the end showing counts of open and closed.
Loop over the last octet from 1 to 20 and ping each address once.
Use a short timeout and suppress output so the sweep finishes quickly.
Print only the addresses that responded, and count them.
Write a script that runs tcpdump filtered to one host passed as an argument.
Add an option to save the capture to a timestamped pcap file.
Add a check that exits with a clear message if the script is not run with enough privileges.
Use curl in a script to fetch only the HTTP status code of a URL.
Write a health check that passes on 200 and fails on anything else.
Extend it to also print how long the request took.
Use openssl in a script to print the expiry date of a site certificate.
Calculate how many days remain until expiry.
Warn when fewer than thirty days remain, and exit non zero.
Use trap so your script cleans up its temporary files even when it fails.
Create temporary files properly instead of using fixed names in the current folder.
Write one error function that prints a message and exits, and use it everywhere.
Write a script that checks nginx is running and its port is listening.
Extend it to fetch the page and confirm the status code is 200.
Add a check that counts errors in the nginx error log from the last hour.
Run a single command on your second VM over SSH from a script.
Loop over both machines and run the same check on each.
Collect the results into one report showing each host and its status.
Write a script that lists every listening port on the machine.
Compare that list against an allowed list stored in an array.
Print a warning for any port that is open but not on the allowed list.
Use a here document to write a multi line block of text into a file.
Insert variables into that block so the output changes per run.
Generate a simple nginx server block from a template using a hostname argument.
Confirm your scripts use key based SSH and never prompt for a password.
Make the script fail clearly when a host is unreachable rather than hanging.
Review every script you have written and confirm none contains a password or key.
Write a function that retries a command up to five times before giving up.
Add a short pause between attempts that grows each time.
Write a script that waits for a port to open before continuing, with a maximum wait.
Store a list of URLs in an array and check each one in a loop.
Append each result to a log file with a timestamp and the status code.
Exit non zero if any check failed, so cron can tell something is wrong.
Combine your best scripts from this month into one toolkit folder with a README.
Run shellcheck across every script and fix every warning.
Give every tool the same argument style and a usage message.
Commit the toolkit to your GitHub repository alongside the day 50 capstone.

questions.prompt: Why put repeated code into a function?
options: You fix a bug in one place instead of several
questions.explanation: Duplication means the same bug exists in several places and you will miss one.

questions.prompt: How does a bash function receive arguments?
options: The same way a script does, as numbered positional parameters
questions.explanation: Inside a function, the numbered parameters refer to the function's own arguments.

questions.prompt: How does a function signal success or failure?
questions.explanation: The return status lets the caller act on the result with an if statement.

questions.prompt: What is an array useful for in a script?
options: Holding a list of items you want to loop over
questions.explanation: It keeps the list in one place so adding an item does not mean new code.

questions.prompt: How do you find the number of items in a bash array?
questions.explanation: The length expansion gives you the count directly.

questions.prompt: Which operator gives the remainder of a division?
questions.explanation: Modulo is useful for anything that repeats on a cycle.

questions.prompt: How many usable hosts does a slash 26 network give you?
questions.explanation: Six host bits give 64 addresses, and two of them are reserved.

questions.prompt: Why write a CIDR table generator instead of memorising the table?
options: Because building it forces you to understand the arithmetic behind it
questions.explanation: You remember what you have had to calculate, not what you have read.

questions.prompt: Why validate an IP address before using it in a script?
options: Because bad input passed to a network command produces confusing failures
questions.explanation: Validating at the edge means the rest of the script can trust its input.

questions.prompt: Where should a function be defined relative to where it is called?
options: Before the point where it is called
At the end of the file
questions.explanation: Bash reads top to bottom, so the definition has to come first.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of one script with three functions over three separate scripts?
options: Shared setup and one place to look for related tools
questions.explanation: Related work belongs together, though very different jobs still deserve separate scripts.

questions.prompt: Why should a function do one thing?
options: Because it is easier to test, reuse and reason about
questions.explanation: A function that does three things is three functions waiting to be separated.

questions.prompt: A bash function can return a status that an if statement can test.
questions.explanation: That is how you build checks that other parts of the script can act on.

questions.prompt: Storing a list in an array means adding an item is a data change rather than a code change.
questions.explanation: That separation is what makes a script easy to extend later.

questions.prompt: Understanding subnetting arithmetic well enough to script it is deeper than memorising a table.
questions.explanation: Scripting it forces the underlying logic to be explicit, which is why the exercise works.

questions.prompt: What is parameter expansion used for?
options: Manipulating strings without calling external tools
questions.explanation: It handles substrings and replacements inside bash itself, which is faster and simpler.

questions.prompt: Why prefer parameter expansion over calling an external command for simple string work?
options: It avoids starting a new process for every operation
questions.explanation: In a loop, spawning processes repeatedly becomes noticeably slow.

questions.prompt: What does awk do best in a script?
options: Selecting and filtering columns from structured output
questions.explanation: Command output is usually columns, and awk is built for exactly that.

questions.prompt: What does sed do best in a script?
questions.explanation: Substitution is its main job, and it works well on config files.

questions.prompt: Why keep a backup when editing a file in place with sed?
options: Because a wrong pattern can corrupt the file with no undo
questions.explanation: In place editing is destructive, and the backup is your only recovery.

questions.prompt: Why check whether a hosts file entry already exists before adding it?
options: So running the script twice does not create duplicates
questions.explanation: This is the same idea as making a script safe to run more than once.

questions.prompt: What should a script do when run with no arguments?
options: Print a usage message and exit non zero
questions.explanation: A usage message is the difference between a tool and a puzzle.

questions.prompt: Why extract only the specific field you need from command output?
options: Because the rest of the output breaks comparisons and conditions
questions.explanation: Scripts need values, and extra text turns a simple check into a broken one.

questions.prompt: What should a gateway check script do if there is no default route?
options: Warn clearly and exit non zero
questions.explanation: Silent success on a broken system is the worst possible outcome.

questions.prompt: Why give a script a default value for its second argument?
options: So the common case works with less typing
questions.explanation: Sensible defaults make a tool pleasant to use without removing flexibility.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of wrapping dig in your own script?
options: You get exactly the output you want in a consistent format
questions.explanation: Wrapping a tool to produce clean, predictable output is a normal thing engineers do.

questions.prompt: Why should output from your tools be easy for another script to consume?
options: Because tools get combined, and messy output breaks the next tool
questions.explanation: This is the same principle as pipes on day 9 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: Editing a system config file from a script without a backup is risky.
questions.explanation: A wrong pattern can break networking or logins with no way back.

questions.prompt: A script that produces different output formats depending on input is easy to build tools on top of.
questions.explanation: Inconsistent output is exactly what makes a tool hard to reuse or chain.

questions.prompt: awk and sed both appeared in the DevOps track and are worth knowing at a basic level only.
questions.explanation: You need enough to select columns and replace text, and Python covers anything more complex.

questions.prompt: Why add a timeout to a port check?
options: So a filtered port does not make the script hang
questions.explanation: Without a timeout the script can sit there indefinitely with nobody watching.

questions.prompt: Why should a check script exit non zero when the check fails?
options: So cron, CI or another script can detect the failure
questions.explanation: The exit code is how automation learns the result.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of checking a list of hosts in a loop?
options: One script covers any number of hosts with no code change
questions.explanation: Adding a host becomes a data change, not a code change.

questions.prompt: Why print a summary at the end of a multi check script?
options: So a human can see the result without reading every line
questions.explanation: The summary is what makes the tool usable in practice.

questions.prompt: Why use a short timeout in a ping sweep?
options: Because most addresses will not respond and waiting for each is slow
questions.explanation: Sweeping twenty addresses with a full default timeout takes far longer than it needs to.

questions.prompt: Why should a tcpdump wrapper check privileges first?
options: Because it will fail confusingly without them
questions.explanation: A clear early message beats a cryptic permission error halfway through.

questions.prompt: How do you get only the HTTP status code from curl?
options: Use the write out option to print just the code
questions.explanation: Curl can output specific fields directly, which avoids fragile parsing.

questions.prompt: What makes a good health check?
options: It returns a clear pass or fail based on the status code
questions.explanation: A health check answers one question, and it should answer it unambiguously.

questions.prompt: Why also measure response time in a health check?
options: Because a slow response is a problem even when the status is 200
questions.explanation: Latency is one of the golden signals, and up is not the same as healthy.

questions.prompt: Why save a capture to a timestamped file?
options: So captures from different runs do not overwrite each other
questions.explanation: This is the same timestamping principle as your backup script.

questions.prompt: Why is a mini port scanner in bash useful even though nmap exists?
options: Because writing it teaches you how the check actually works
questions.explanation: You use nmap at work, and you build the small version to understand it.

questions.prompt: What should you do with a script that hangs instead of failing?
options: Add a timeout so it fails cleanly
questions.explanation: A hanging script in cron is worse than one that fails, because nothing reports it.

questions.prompt: A health check that always exits zero is useless to automation.
questions.explanation: Nothing downstream can distinguish a healthy service from a broken one.

questions.prompt: Scripts that check things should be safe to run repeatedly without side effects.
questions.explanation: Checks are run constantly, so a check that changes something is a hazard.

questions.prompt: Building small versions of tools you will later use professionally is wasted effort.
questions.explanation: Building the small version is how you understand what the professional tool is doing.

questions.prompt: Why check certificate expiry from a script?
options: Because expired certificates cause outages and the warning comes too late by hand
questions.explanation: Certificate expiry is one of the most common avoidable outages there is.

questions.prompt: Why warn thirty days before expiry rather than on the day?
options: Because renewal takes time and coordination
questions.explanation: A warning on the expiry day is not a warning, it is a notification of an outage.

questions.prompt: What does trap do in a script?
options: Runs cleanup code when the script exits or is interrupted
questions.explanation: It ensures temporary files are removed even when things go wrong.

questions.prompt: Why create temporary files properly rather than using a fixed name?
options: Because two runs at once would collide and overwrite each other
questions.explanation: Fixed names also make a script predictable to anyone trying to interfere with it.

questions.prompt: Why have one error function used everywhere?
options: So every failure looks the same and always exits properly
questions.explanation: Consistent failure handling is what makes a script trustworthy.

questions.prompt: What should a web server check verify?
options: That the service runs, the port listens and the page returns 200
questions.explanation: A running process that serves errors is still an outage.

questions.prompt: Why count recent errors rather than all errors in a log?
options: Because old errors are not evidence of a current problem
questions.explanation: A count since the beginning of time tells you nothing about right now.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a remote host is unreachable during an SSH check?
options: It reports the failure clearly and moves on
questions.explanation: One unreachable host should not stop you checking the others.

questions.prompt: Why should scripts use key based SSH rather than passwords?
options: Because a script cannot type a password and stored passwords are a risk
questions.explanation: This is the same reasoning as day 15 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: What is a firewall audit script actually comparing?
options: Ports that are open against ports that should be open
questions.explanation: The gap between intended and actual is where security problems live.

questions.prompt: Why should you review old scripts for secrets?
options: Because a password written early on stays in the file and in git history
questions.explanation: Secrets committed once are effectively published, as you learned on day 88.

questions.prompt: What makes a report from a multi host check useful?
options: One line per host showing its status clearly
questions.explanation: You want to see the whole picture at a glance, including what is fine.

questions.prompt: A script that leaves temporary files behind after failing is poorly written.
questions.explanation: Cleanup on failure is exactly what trap exists to guarantee.

questions.prompt: Comparing open ports against an allowed list is a simple form of the drift detection idea.
questions.explanation: It is the same concept as Terraform drift, applied to firewall state.

questions.prompt: A password stored in a script is acceptable if the script is only on your own machine.
questions.explanation: Machines get shared, backed up and committed, and the habit itself is the problem.

questions.prompt: What does a here document let you do?
options: Write a multi line block of text into a file or command
questions.explanation: It is the cleanest way to generate a config file from a script.

questions.prompt: Why insert variables into a generated config file?
options: So one template produces the right config for any hostname or port
questions.explanation: This is templating, and it is the same idea Terraform and Ansible use at a larger scale.

questions.prompt: Why add retry logic to a command that talks to the network?
options: Because transient failures are normal and a single attempt is fragile
questions.explanation: A retry turns a temporary blip into a non event.

questions.prompt: Why increase the pause between retries?
options: To avoid hammering a service that is already struggling
questions.explanation: Backing off gives the other side a chance to recover.

questions.prompt: Why does a wait loop need a maximum wait?
options: Because otherwise it can block forever when something is truly broken
questions.explanation: An unbounded wait is a hang, and hangs are invisible in automation.

questions.prompt: Why log each monitoring result with a timestamp?
options: So you can see when a problem started and how long it lasted
questions.explanation: Duration and start time are the first questions asked about any incident.

questions.prompt: Why should a monitoring script exit non zero if any check failed?
options: So the thing running it knows something is wrong
questions.explanation: The exit code is the only signal an automated runner reliably sees.

questions.prompt: Why give every tool in a toolkit the same argument style?
options: So you can use any of them without re reading the source
questions.explanation: Consistency is what makes a collection of scripts feel like a real toolkit.

questions.prompt: Why run shellcheck across every script before committing?
options: Because most of its warnings are real bugs waiting to happen
questions.explanation: Quoting and unset variable problems are exactly what it finds.

questions.prompt: What makes a scripts repository worth showing an employer?
options: Small, well written tools that each solve a real problem, with a README
questions.explanation: Readable and useful beats clever, and the README is what gets read first.

questions.prompt: What have you actually been practising all month?
options: Automating the networking work from the main track
questions.explanation: The second track exists to turn the first track into things that run by themselves.

questions.prompt: Why keep this track to thirty minutes a day?
options: So it never eats the time the main track needs
questions.explanation: Two tracks only work if the smaller one stays genuinely small.

questions.prompt: Generating config files from a template in bash is a simplified version of what larger tools do.
questions.explanation: The concept scales up directly into the tooling you meet later.

questions.prompt: A monitoring script with no maximum wait and no timeout is safe to schedule in cron.
questions.explanation: It can hang indefinitely, and nothing will tell you that it did.

questions.prompt: By the end of this month you should have a small set of tools you actually use.
questions.explanation: Tools you use are the ones you remember, and they are also the ones worth showing.
